questions.question_text: The calculated spin only magnetic moment of $\text{Cr}^{2+}$ ion is
questions.question_html: The calculated spin only magnetic moment of $\text{Cr}^{2+}$ ion is
questions.explanation_text: For spin only magnetic moment, we use the formula $\mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)}\text{BM}$ where $n$ is the number of unpaired electrons. Chromium has atomic number $24$ . Its electronic configuration is $\text{Cr}=[\text{Ar}]3d^{5}4s^{1}$ For $\text{Cr}^{2+}$ , two electrons are removed. First the $4s$ electron is removed, then one electron from $3d$ . So, $\text{Cr}^{2+}=[\text{Ar}]3d^{4}$ In $3d^{4}$ , according to Hund’s rule, the four electrons occupy four different $d$ orbitals singly. So the number of unpaired electrons is $n=4$ Now, $\mu=\sqrt{4(4+2)}$ $\mu=\sqrt{24}$ $\mu=4.90\text{BM}$ So the correct answer is $4.90\text{BM}$ Option B.
questions.explanation_html:
For spin only magnetic moment, we use the formula

$\mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)}\text{BM}$

where $n$ is the number of unpaired electrons.

Chromium has atomic number $24$ .

Its electronic configuration is

$\text{Cr}=[\text{Ar}]3d^{5}4s^{1}$

For $\text{Cr}^{2+}$ , two electrons are removed. First the $4s$ electron is removed, then one electron from $3d$ .

So,

$\text{Cr}^{2+}=[\text{Ar}]3d^{4}$

In $3d^{4}$ , according to Hund’s rule, the four electrons occupy four different $d$ orbitals singly.

So the number of unpaired electrons is

$n=4$

Now,

$\mu=\sqrt{4(4+2)}$

$\mu=\sqrt{24}$

$\mu=4.90\text{BM}$

So the correct answer is

$4.90\text{BM}$

Option B.

questions.question_text: The highest oxidation state of manganese in fluoride is $+4$ ( $\text{MnF}_{4}$ ), but the highest oxidation state in oxides is $+7$ ( $\text{Mn}_{2}\text{O}_{7}$ ), because
questions.question_html: The highest oxidation state of manganese in fluoride is $+4$ ( $\text{MnF}_{4}$ ), but the highest oxidation state in oxides is $+7$ ( $\text{Mn}_{2}\text{O}_{7}$ ), because

options.label: A
options.text: Fluorine is more electronegative than oxygen
options.html: Fluorine is more electronegative than oxygen

options.label: B
options.html: Fluorine possesses d-orbitals

options.label: C
options.html: Fluorine stabilises lower oxidation state

options.label: D
options.text: In covalent compounds, fluorine can form single bond only, while oxygen forms double bond
options.html: In covalent compounds, fluorine can form single bond only, while oxygen forms double bond

questions.explanation_text: The correct option is Option D . In $\text{MnF}_{4}$ , fluorine has oxidation state $-1$ . So, if oxidation state of Mn is $x$ : $x+4(-1)=0$ $x=+4$ So manganese shows $+4$ oxidation state in $\text{MnF}_{4}$ . In $\text{Mn}_{2}\text{O}_{7}$ , oxygen has oxidation state $-2$ . Let oxidation state of Mn be $x$ : $2x+7(-2)=0$ $2x-14=0$ $x=+7$ So manganese shows $+7$ oxidation state in $\text{Mn}_{2}\text{O}_{7}$ . Now the main reason is bonding. Fluorine is very electronegative, but it can form only one single bond because it needs only one electron to complete its octet. So fluorine cannot form multiple bonds with manganese. Due to this, it cannot stabilise very high oxidation states like $+7$ in manganese. Oxygen, on the other hand, can form double bonds with metals. These multiple bonds help stabilise higher oxidation states. That is why manganese can show $+7$ oxidation state in oxides like $\text{Mn}_{2}\text{O}_{7}$ . So the correct reason is: Option D: In covalent compounds, fluorine can form single bond only, while oxygen forms double bond.
questions.explanation_html:
The correct option is Option D.

In $\text{MnF}_{4}$ , fluorine has oxidation state $-1$ .

So, if oxidation state of Mn is $x$ :

$x+4(-1)=0$

$x=+4$

So manganese shows $+4$ oxidation state in $\text{MnF}_{4}$ .

In $\text{Mn}_{2}\text{O}_{7}$ , oxygen has oxidation state $-2$ .

Let oxidation state of Mn be $x$ :

$2x+7(-2)=0$

$2x-14=0$

$x=+7$

So manganese shows $+7$ oxidation state in $\text{Mn}_{2}\text{O}_{7}$ .

Now the main reason is bonding.

Fluorine is very electronegative, but it can form only one single bond because it needs only one electron to complete its octet. So fluorine cannot form multiple bonds with manganese. Due to this, it cannot stabilise very high oxidation states like $+7$ in manganese.

Oxygen, on the other hand, can form double bonds with metals. These multiple bonds help stabilise higher oxidation states. That is why manganese can show $+7$ oxidation state in oxides like $\text{Mn}_{2}\text{O}_{7}$ .

So the correct reason is:

Option D: In covalent compounds, fluorine can form single bond only, while oxygen forms double bond.

questions.question_text: Which of the following will not act as an oxidising agent?
questions.question_html: Which of the following will not act as an oxidising agent?
questions.explanation_text: $\text{MoO}_{3}$ will not act as an oxidising agent. So, the correct option is: $\text{Option B}\text{MoO}_{3}$ In all the given species, the metal is in the $+6$ oxidation state. For chromium: $\text{CrO}_{3},\text{CrO}_{4}^{2-},\text{Cr}_{2}\text{O}_{7}^{2-}$ chromium is in the $+6$ oxidation state. Chromium in $+6$ state is easily reduced to $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ , especially in acidic medium. So these compounds behave as strong oxidising agents. For example, dichromate ion gets reduced as: $\text{Cr}_{2}\text{O}_{7}^{2-} \longrightarrow \text{Cr}^{3+}$ Hence, $\text{CrO}_{3}$ , $\text{CrO}_{4}^{2-}$ and $\text{Cr}_{2}\text{O}_{7}^{2-}$ act as oxidising agents. But in $\text{MoO}_{3}$ , molybdenum is also in the $+6$ state, and this state is comparatively more stable for molybdenum. It does not get reduced easily, so $\text{MoO}_{3}$ does not normally act as an oxidising agent. Hence: $\text{MoO}_{3}$

The electronic configuration of Cerium ( $Ce$ ) is: $Ce:[Xe]4f^{1}5d^{1}6s^{2}$ When Cerium is in the +4 oxidation state ( $Ce^{+4}$ ), it has the electronic configuration: $Ce^{+4}:[Xe]4f^{0}5d^{0}6s^{0}$ In this state, Cerium has a stable noble gas configuration, which is why it is well-known to exhibit a +4 oxidation state.
questions.explanation_html:
The Lanthanoid series element known for exhibiting a +4 oxidation state is Cerium.

The electronic configuration of Cerium ( $Ce$ ) is:

$Ce:[Xe]4f^{1}5d^{1}6s^{2}$

When Cerium is in the +4 oxidation state ( $Ce^{+4}$ ), it has the electronic configuration:

$Ce^{+4}:[Xe]4f^{0}5d^{0}6s^{0}$

In this state, Cerium has a stable noble gas configuration, which is why it is well-known to exhibit a +4 oxidation state.

questions.question_html: In the following pairs, the one in which both transition metal ions are colourless is
questions.explanation_text: In transition metal ions, the coloration typically depends on the presence of unpaired electrons in the d-orbitals. Ions with either completely empty d-orbitals ( $d^{0}$ ) or fully filled d-orbitals ( $d^{10}$ ) do not exhibit d-d transitions, which are responsible for colored compounds. As a result, these ions tend to be colorless. The $Sc^{3+}$ ion has the electron configuration $[Ar]3d^{0}$ , meaning its d-orbitals are empty. The $Zn^{2+}$ ion has the electron configuration $[Ar]3d^{10}$ , indicating fully filled d-orbitals. Since both $Sc^{3+}$ and $Zn^{2+}$ lack the d-d electron transitions necessary for color, they are colorless.
questions.explanation_html:
In transition metal ions, the coloration typically depends on the presence of unpaired electrons in the d-orbitals. Ions with either completely empty d-orbitals ( $d^{0}$ ) or fully filled d-orbitals ( $d^{10}$ ) do not exhibit d-d transitions, which are responsible for colored compounds. As a result, these ions tend to be colorless.

The $Sc^{3+}$ ion has the electron configuration $[Ar]3d^{0}$ , meaning its d-orbitals are empty.

The $Zn^{2+}$ ion has the electron configuration $[Ar]3d^{10}$ , indicating fully filled d-orbitals.

Since both $Sc^{3+}$ and $Zn^{2+}$ lack the d-d electron transitions necessary for color, they are colorless.

questions.explanation_text: In general, the melting points of transition elements increases across a period from left to right due to increasing atomic number and the corresponding increase in effective nuclear charge. Among the elements mentioned in the options, chromium $(Cr)$ has a higher melting point compared to manganese $(Mn)$ . questions.question_html: What will be the value of $x$ in $Fe^{x+}$ , if the magnetic moment, $\mu=\sqrt{24}BM$ ?
questions.explanation_text: Given that, magnetic moment, $\mu=\sqrt{24}$ and $\mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)}$ where, $n=$ unpaired electrons $\begin{aligned} \sqrt{24} & =\sqrt{n(n+2)} \\ 24 & =n(n+2)=n^{2}+2n \\ n^{2}+2n-24 & =0 \Rightarrow n^{2}+6n-4n-24=0 \\ n(n+6)-4(n+6) & =0 \Rightarrow (n-4)(n+6)=0 \\ n & =4,-6 \end{aligned}$ $\therefore$ Number of unpaired electrons $=4$ If oxidation of $F$ is +2 then it has 4 unpaired electrons.
questions.explanation_html:
Given that, magnetic moment, $\mu=\sqrt{24}$

and $\mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)}$

where, $n=$ unpaired electrons

$\begin{aligned} \sqrt{24} & =\sqrt{n(n+2)} \\ 24 & =n(n+2)=n^{2}+2n \\ n^{2}+2n-24 & =0 \Rightarrow n^{2}+6n-4n-24=0 \\ n(n+6)-4(n+6) & =0 \Rightarrow (n-4)(n+6)=0 \\ n & =4,-6 \end{aligned}$

$\therefore$ Number of unpaired electrons $=4$

questions.question_text: Which of the following oxides shows electrical properties like metals?
questions.question_html: Which of the following oxides shows electrical properties like metals?
questions.explanation_text: The correct answer is Option D: $CrO_{2}.$ Here’s why: $SiO_{2}$ (silicon dioxide) has a network covalent structure, making it an electrical insulator rather than a conductor. $MgO$ (magnesium oxide) is an ionic compound with a large band gap. Such materials typically do not conduct electricity. $SO_{2}(s)$ —if it exists in solid form—is not known for metallic conductivity; it is generally not considered to have the conduction properties of metals. $CrO_{2}$ (chromium dioxide), on the other hand, is a well-known metallic oxide. It possesses unique properties such as half-metallicity, meaning electrons in one spin channel contribute to electrical conduction. This gives $CrO_{2}$ metallic-like electrical conductivity, which is why it is used in magnetic recording and related applications. Thus, $CrO_{2}$ is the oxide that shows electrical properties similar to metals.
questions.explanation_html:
The correct answer is Option D: $CrO_{2}.$

Here’s why:

$SiO_{2}$ (silicon dioxide) has a network covalent structure, making it an electrical insulator rather than a conductor.

$MgO$ (magnesium oxide) is an ionic compound with a large band gap. Such materials typically do not conduct electricity.

$SO_{2}(s)$ —if it exists in solid form—is not known for metallic conductivity; it is generally not considered to have the conduction properties of metals.

$CrO_{2}$ (chromium dioxide), on the other hand, is a well-known metallic oxide. It possesses unique properties such as half-metallicity, meaning electrons in one spin channel contribute to electrical conduction. This gives $CrO_{2}$ metallic-like electrical conductivity, which is why it is used in magnetic recording and related applications.

Thus, $CrO_{2}$ is the oxide that shows electrical properties similar to metals.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statement is wrong regarding lanthanoids?
questions.question_html: Which of the following statement is wrong regarding lanthanoids?

options.label: A
options.text: $Ln$ (III) compounds are predominantly ionic in character.
options.html: $Ln$ (III) compounds are predominantly ionic in character.

options.label: B
options.html: $Ln$ (III) compounds are generally colourless.

options.label: C
options.text: $Ln$ (III) hydroxides are mainly basic in nature.
options.html: $Ln$ (III) hydroxides are mainly basic in nature.

options.label: D
options.text: The inoic size of $Ln(III)$ ions decreases with increasing atomic number.
options.html: The inoic size of $Ln(III)$ ions decreases with increasing atomic number.

questions.explanation_text: The explanation concerns the properties of lanthanoids, specifically focusing on $Ln$ (III) ions. Here is a more refined and professional explanation: The $Ln$ (III) ions, due to their relatively large size, typically form compounds where the bonding is predominantly ionic. These $Ln$ (III) compounds are generally colorful. This coloration is due to electronic transitions within the f-orbitals. Hydroxides of $Ln$ (III) are mainly basic. This basicity is a characteristic of the hydroxides formed by these large, charged ions. As you move across the lanthanoid series (increasing atomic number), the ionic size of the $Ln$ (III) ions decreases. This trend is known as the lanthanoid contraction, and it occurs because the addition of electrons in f-orbitals does not effectively shield the increasing nuclear charge from the outer electrons.

The explanation concerns the properties of lanthanoids, specifically focusing on $Ln$ (III) ions. Here is a more refined and professional explanation:

The $Ln$ (III) ions, due to their relatively large size, typically form compounds where the bonding is predominantly ionic.

These $Ln$ (III) compounds are generally colorful. This coloration is due to electronic transitions within the f-orbitals.

Hydroxides of $Ln$ (III) are mainly basic. This basicity is a characteristic of the hydroxides formed by these large, charged ions.

As you move across the lanthanoid series (increasing atomic number), the ionic size of the $Ln$ (III) ions decreases. This trend is known as the lanthanoid contraction, and it occurs because the addition of electrons in f-orbitals does not effectively shield the increasing nuclear charge from the outer electrons.
